name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey places religious organizations within the broader "Other services" category under NAICS 81, where 12.6 percent of firms reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 11.3 percent in the prior period. This is the closest official measure available for the sector, and because religious organizations share that category with other service firms, the figure should be read as an approximation rather than a precise count of congregations deploying AI.

The clearest window into what AI actually looks like inside congregations comes from Gloo, a technology platform used by thousands of US churches. Per Gloo, faith-based organizations are using AI for ministry workflows, data-informed decision-making, and what the company calls "missional intelligence," with tools spanning inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows. Gloo also offers an evaluation framework that measures AI alignment across seven dimensions of human flourishing, reflecting a sector concern that general-purpose models may not reflect the values of religious communities. The Barna Group, whose research tracks AI adoption and perception among US ministry leaders, reports that nearly all pastors worry AI could misread scripture, and most want AI to present every interpretation of a difficult passage rather than settle on one, suggesting that where adoption is happening, it is proceeding cautiously and with strong theological guardrails.

Theological concern about AI's role in worship itself is a consistent theme across the sources. A University of Notre Dame professor of philosophy leading a research project on AI and religion, cited by Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, stated that using AI to draft anything spoken in worship reflects a basic misunderstanding of what Christians believe is happening when a preacher delivers a homily. That framing helps explain why adoption may be concentrated in administrative and preparatory tasks rather than in the act of preaching or pastoral care itself.

The ethics infrastructure around this sector is more developed than in many industries. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, works to bring the values of the world's major religious traditions into debates about AI development, arguing that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation, these questions are not merely technical but spiritual. The organization convenes technologists, theologians, and ethicists specifically to shape AI development in ways it describes as "life-affirming." The Hartford Institute for Religion Research, with 45 years of tracking congregational life, and Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life work both monitor how clergy and the broader public view technology in religious spaces, providing longitudinal context as attitudes shift.

For a congregation or faith organization considering deployment, the sourced evidence points to a sector that is measurably adopting AI but doing so with unusual attention to the boundaries of that use. Administrative tasks, communication, and data workflows appear to be the practical entry points, while sermon writing and pastoral functions remain contested territory on theological grounds. The existence of purpose-built platforms like Gloo, and the active ethics work of organizations like AI and Faith and Notre Dame's institute, means that decision-makers have more sector-specific guidance available than the raw adoption numbers alone would suggest, though rigorous published ROI data for this sector does not appear in the sources reviewed.
